paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A historian recently pointed out a similarity between musicians and scientists. Most musicians describe their work as experiments — a series of efforts designed to explore a shared concern or to establish a viewpoint. A Canadian academic has added that the work of both scientists and musicians involves similar stages of development: an initial creative stage, followed by testing and refining stages that typically use clearly established procedures, but also require further creative input. Both groups are also prepared and happy to have their work viewed differently by different people. However, for the musician, the goal of musical composition is to get across an aspect of a universal truth that, if successful, will continue to move and to touch people for generations. For the scientist, on the other hand, the goal of a theory is to convey 'truth for now' — accepting that someday their theory will be replaced by new ideas, because that is the way science advances.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: However, music is unusual both for the fact that it is found everywhere and that it always has been. No known culture now or any time in the recorded past has lacked music. Some of the oldest physical artefacts found in human excavation sites are musical instruments: bone flutes and animal skins stretched over hollow tree stumps to make drums. Whenever people come together for any special reason, music is there: weddings, stadium sporting events, a romantic dinner and so on. Even more so in non-industrialised cultures than in modern Western societies, music is and was of great importance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There is a story of an American professor of anthropology who performed fieldwork with the Sotho people in southern Africa. There, studying and interacting with local villagers, he patiently earned their trust until one day he was asked to join in one of their songs, at which point he said 'I don't sing'. The villagers found his objection puzzling and inexplicable. The Sotho consider singing a commonplace activity performed by everyone, young and old, men and women — not an activity reserved for a special few. To the professor, a public display of singing and dancing would have implied he thought himself an expert. But to the villagers, as he later explained, 'It was as odd to them as if I'd told them that I couldn't walk, even though I have both my legs.' Singing and dancing were natural activities in everybody's lives. Their verb for singing, as in many of the world's languages, also means to dance; there is no distinction, since it is assumed that singing involves bodily movement.

The Sotho consider singing a commonplace activity performed by everyone, young and old, men and women — not an activity reserved for a special few.

To the professor, a public display of singing and dancing would have implied he thought himself an expert. But to the villagers, as he later explained, 'It was as odd to them as if I'd told them that I couldn't walk, even though I have both my legs.' Singing and dancing were natural activities in everybody's lives. Their verb for singing, as in many of the world's languages, also means to dance; there is no distinction, since it is assumed that singing involves bodily movement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A couple of generations ago, before television, many western families would sit around and play music together for entertainment. Nowadays there is a great emphasis on technique and skill, and whether a musician is 'good enough' to play for others. Music-making has become a somewhat reserved activity, practised by only a few, and the rest listen. The music industry is massive in the United States, employing thousands of people and generating billions of dollars in income. As a result of the exposure to music that this brings, most Americans would appear to have become expert music listeners, even if few of them actually play an instrument these days. They have acquired the cognitive capacity to detect wrong notes, to find music they enjoy, to remember hundreds of melodies, and to tap their feet in time with the music — an activity that involves a process of meter extraction so complicated that most computers cannot do it. And all this happens simply as a result of listening. But why do they do it, and why are they willing to spend so much on it? Concert tickets, for example, are far from cheap. Is it wired into us to do so?

And all this happens simply as a result of listening. But why do they do it, and why are they willing to spend so much on it? Concert tickets, for example, are far from cheap. Is it wired into us to do so?

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Contrary to the old, simplistic notion that art and music are processed in the right hemisphere of our brains, with language and mathematics in the left hemisphere, recent findings are showing that musical awareness is distributed throughout the brain. Some patients, for example, who have lost the ability to read a newspaper, can still read music, or some individuals who lack the motor coordination to button their own sweater can, remarkably, still play the piano. Music listening, playing, and composing engage nearly every area of the brain that we have so far identified, and involve nearly every neural subsystem. Could this fact account for claims that music listening is the equivalent of exercising our minds; that listening to the music of the famous Austrian genius Mozart 20 minutes a day will make us smarter?

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The magic of music is harnessed by advertising executives, filmmakers, parents and others. Advertisers use music to make a soft drink, running shoe or car seem more desirable than that of their competitors. Film directors use music to tell us how to interpret scenes that otherwise might be ambiguous, or to heighten how we feel at particularly dramatic times. Think of a typical chase in a thriller, or the music that might accompany a lone individual climbing a staircase in a dark old mansion: music is being used to manipulate our emotions, and we tend to accept, if not outright enjoy, the power of music to make us experience these. Nothing else could move us so effectively.
